text.p: Senior energy officials from EU states began a two-day meeting in Brussels on Tuesday to tackle the main outstanding obstacles to a deal to open up the European Union gas market.

It is the first top level debate on a compromise proposal from the Dutch EU presidency designed to narrow the differences between countries pushing for fast and far-reaching liberalisation and those who are more sceptical.
EU officials said the outcome of the meeting would show what chances there were of EU energy ministers reaching a political agreement on gas liberalisation this year.

The Dutch had hoped energy ministers would be able to reach a provisional accord when they meet in Brussels on May 26 but this now appears unlikely since France and possibly Ireland will be in the throes of general elections and will be unwilling or unable to make a firm decision.

This week's talks are expected to focus on the extent to which national markets will have to open up, unbundling of accounts, connections to offshore installations, and how to handle long term take-or-pay contracts -- which dominate Europe's gas industry.

Take-or-pay contracts are one of the thorniest issues, with differences of opinion partly reflecting the fact that only Britain and the Netherlands produce and export gas, while other member states are big importers.
With the EU's dependence on outside gas suppliers in Russia, Algeria and Norway forecast to rise from 40 to 70 percent by 2020, the industry is loathe to abandon the security of long term contracts.
Countries like Portugal, Finland and Greece which are only now setting up their gas markets are also keen to protect the sector from all-out competition, at least during the initial stages.

Like the European Commission, the Dutch presidency is arguing that if take-or-pay contracts are to continue to characterise the EU market for the forseeable future then they must become more flexible and allow for more competition than at present.
"We have to have diversity of supply as well as security of supply," an EU diplomat told Reuters on Tuesday.

Europe could not tell Russia or Algeria to open their markets but it could force gas purchasers in the EU to increase the number of their suppliers, he said, adding that Russia's state gas monopoly Gazprom had controlling stakes in 25 percent of Europe's gas industry.

A copy of the Dutch proposal obtained by Reuters says future take-or-pay contracts should contain a price revision clause and should only be allowed to limit the level of competition in the market in specific, exceptional circumstances.
The member states remain divided over who should authorise these requests to limit competition.

One possible compromise under discussion is to let national governments rule on existing take-or-pay contracts, after notifying the Commission, but submit all decisions from 1997 onwards for approval by Brussels.
The member states continue to disagree too on the extent to which the gas market should be liberalised.
The Dutch compromise suggests they should initially liberalise 30 percent of their national markets, bringing this up to 50 percent over 10 years, though the figures remain controversial.
There is no agreement either over whether distributors will be allowed, like large industrial gas consumers, to negotiate contracts directly with external gas suppliers.
Germany and Britain, for instance, want the definition of so-called "eligible customers" to include distributors but France opposes the idea, the official said.
